name: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
teaser: 1967 Beatles, recorded in 6 months at Abbey Road. The first rock album to win Album of the Year at the Grammys — and the first record people actually listened to as a coherent whole.

exploreAction.instruction: Skip the title track — it's a four-bar overture. Start with 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' and notice how the bassline changes time signature three times without announcing it. The album's structure is symmetrical: side 1 ends with 'A Day in the Life', side 2 with a reprise.

tracks.title: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
With a Little Help from My Friends
Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds
Being for the Benefit of Mr. Kite!
Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (Reprise)

synopsis: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967) is the record that turned the pop album into an art form. The Beatles had stopped touring the year before, so they no longer had to write songs they could play live; they could build music entirely in the studio. Over six months at Abbey Road they layered tape loops, sped-up and slowed-down vocals, music hall brass, a 40-piece orchestra and sound effects into something nobody had heard before. The album presents itself as a performance by a fictional band, which freed them to write as characters: the soldier's loneliness in 'A Day in the Life', the nostalgia of 'When I'm Sixty-Four', the Indian drone of 'Within You Without You'. The famous cover, a collage of famous faces around the band in marching-band uniforms, was staged by Peter Blake and cost more than the recording sessions themselves. It won Album of the Year at the Grammys, the first rock album to do so, and spent over a year on the British chart. More than any single song, it made listeners hear the album itself as the work of art, the idea that a record could be one long, continuous statement.

name: Abbey Road
teaser: 1969 — the last album the Beatles recorded together. The side-B medley (tracks 7–17) was never rehearsed as a single sequence; George Martin stitched it together over one long session.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to side B as a single 23-minute piece. The medley's transitions were never rehearsed — Lennon and McCartney wrote each fragment in isolation. Then listen again and count how many times you hear the phrase 'golden slumbers' return in different keys.

tracks.title: You Never Give Me Your Money
She Came In Through the Bathroom Window

synopsis: Abbey Road (1969) turned out to be the last album the Beatles recorded, and in many ways it is their most graceful goodbye. By the summer of 1969 the four of them were barely on speaking terms, and the sessions were tense, yet the music they made has a warmth and confidence that their previous sessions lacked. The first side is a collection of individual songs, from the hard riff of 'Come Together' and George Harrison's 'Something', which Frank Sinatra called the greatest love song of the past fifty years, to the heavy, unfinished-sounding 'I Want You (She's So Heavy)'. The second side is the reason the album is remembered: a continuous medley of song fragments stitched together, eight pieces flowing from one to the next with no gap, ending in the soaring 'The End'. The cover photo of the four of them walking across the zebra crossing outside the studio became one of the most imitated images in music. Recorded in one of the most productive months of their career, it was released in September 1969, less than a year before the band announced their split.

name: The Dark Side of the Moon
teaser: Pink Floyd 1973 — spent 937 weeks on the Billboard 200. Recorded partly live at Abbey Road with a rotary speaker custom-built for the sessions. The opening heartbeat is Roger Waters tapping a clock in time with his own pulse.

exploreAction.targetName: The Dark Side of the Moon (1973) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen on headphones in a dark room. The album is a single 43-minute arc with no breaks between songs. Notice how Clare Torry's improvised vocal on 'The Great Gig in the Sky' was a single take — she was paid £30 and later won a settlement for co-writing credit.

tracks.title: The Great Gig in the Sky

synopsis: The Dark Side of the Moon (1973) is the album that made Pink Floyd one of the biggest bands on earth and stayed on the Billboard 200 chart for 937 weeks, over seventeen years. It grew out of a piece the band had been playing live since early 1972, honed in concert before they ever recorded it, and the lyrics, mostly by Roger Waters, circle one theme: the pressures that can drive a person mad, from time and money to war and death. The band recorded it at Abbey Road with engineer Alan Parsons, and it is famous for its sound effects, all of them real: a heartbeat, a cash register, clocks recorded in an antiques shop, and fragments of conversation from people asked about death and violence. The songs bleed into one another without gaps, so the album works as a single continuous piece, from the opening heartbeat and the screaming of 'On the Run' to the soaring 'The Great Gig in the Sky', where Clare Torry's wordless vocal was improvised in one session. The cover, a beam of white light passing through a prism, was designed by Hipgnosis and is one of the most recognizable images in music. It is the rare album that is both a technical marvel and a deeply felt record about being human.

name: Led Zeppelin IV
teaser: 1971 — never officially titled. The band were so annoyed by critics after Led Zeppelin III that they refused to put their name on the cover. Has 'Stairway to Heaven', the most-played rock song in FM radio history.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Stairway' three times. The famous opening — Plant improvised the lyrics, Page edited them. Three movements: acoustic intro, electric interlude, hard-rock climax. Then 'When the Levee Breaks' — Bonham recorded his drums in a stairwell at Headley Grange.

synopsis: Led Zeppelin IV (1971), sometimes called Zoso or the untitled album, is the record that made Led Zeppelin the biggest band in the world. After critics dismissed their third album, the band refused to put a title or their name on the cover, printing only four mysterious symbols chosen by each member. They recorded it partly in a house called Headley Grange in the English countryside, using the Rolling Stones' mobile studio, which gave the songs a loose, live-in-room feel. The album runs from the pounding 'Black Dog' to the folk-rock of 'Going to California' and the apocalyptic blues of 'When the Levee Breaks', whose huge drum sound was captured by recording John Bonham at the bottom of a stairwell. In the middle sits 'Stairway to Heaven', eight minutes that build from a quiet acoustic guitar to a screaming solo, a song so ubiquitous that it became a rite of passage for guitarists everywhere. The band never released it as a single, yet it became one of the most played songs in radio history. The album sold over twenty million copies and turned the group from a heavy blues band into an institution.

name: Nevermind
teaser: Nirvana's 1991 second album — recorded for $65,000, sold 30 million copies, ended hair metal in 18 months. Butch Vig produced it; Kurt insisted the guitars sound both huge and broken at the same time.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening 4 bars of 'Smells Like Teen Spirit'. Cobain's voice is barely audible for half the verse, then explodes. That contrast — quiet verse into screamed chorus — became the template for 1990s rock. Now listen to 'Something in the Way' — recorded with Kurt lying on the studio floor.

synopsis: Nevermind (1991) is the album that ended the 1980s in popular music. Nirvana's second record was recorded in Los Angeles with producer Butch Vig, who gave Kurt Cobain's songs a bright, radio-sized sound without sanding off their edges. The band had spent years in the underground, and the record's huge success took them completely by surprise: 'Smells Like Teen Spirit', with its verse-chorus-quiet-loud structure and a riff that sounded like the Pixies played through a Marshall stack, became an anthem for a generation that felt ignored. By January 1992 it had knocked Michael Jackson's Dangerous off the top of the Billboard chart, and the album eventually sold over thirty million copies. The cover, a baby swimming underwater toward a dollar bill on a fishhook, was an accident of a photo shoot that became one of the defining images of the era. The album's real subject is confusion, anger and alienation, wrapped in hooks so strong that most listeners only felt the joy of them at first.

name: OK Computer
teaser: Radiohead 1997 — recorded partly in a mansion in St Catherine's-on-the-Hudson, partly in a barn with a jazz band. The album that defined post-millennial British rock and made Thom Yorke the unwilling voice of a generation.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Airbag' through 'Lucky' — that's the first half. Then listen to 'Lucky' again. The lyrics 'I'm up late' and 'a pop song' mean something different once you know the album was recorded in a borrowed mansion while Radiohead were falling apart. The last track 'The Tourist' is Thom alone at a piano.

synopsis: OK Computer (1997) is Radiohead's anxious masterpiece about life in a world run by machines, deadlines, airports and advertising. The band wrote it after years of relentless touring, and the songs reflect their exhaustion and unease: they recorded much of it in a large, echoing country house in England called St Catherine's Court, where the natural acoustics shaped the sound. Unlike their earlier guitar rock, the music here is built from layers, with Jonny Greenwood's treated guitar, Thom Yorke's falsetto, and strange details like a fax machine in the mix and a computer-synthesized voice reciting instructions in the middle of 'Fitter Happier'. The lyrics circle themes of isolation and modern alienation: the six-minute 'Paranoid Android' moves through several movements like a miniature suite, 'Karma Police' is a paranoid fantasy of revenge, and 'No Surprises' is a lullaby about a life of quiet desperation. It won the Grammy for Best Alternative Album and is regularly named one of the greatest records of the 1990s, the moment a rock band turned the anxiety of the digital age into something beautiful and strange.

name: In Utero
teaser: Nirvana's 1993 third album — Steve Albini recorded it in 5 days in Cannon Falls, Minnesota. Cobain didn't like the rawness; the label remixed 3 songs. It still went to #1, proving a band could be abrasive and commercial simultaneously.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Serve the Servants' — Cobain names the album's position in his life ('Teenage angst has paid off well'). Then 'All Apologies' — the chord progression moves in fourths, not fifths. Albini miked the drums from 20 feet away to get that cavernous sound.

tracks.title: Frances Farmer Will Have Her Revenge on Seattle

synopsis: In Utero (1993) is Nirvana's raw, difficult follow-up to Nevermind, the album where Kurt Cobain tried to get away from the glossy sound that had made them famous. He insisted on recording with Steve Albini, a producer known for capturing bands live and harsh, and the sessions took place in a studio in rural Minnesota in under two weeks. The title means 'in the womb', and the album is full of bodily imagery, blood and illness and birth, wrapped in some of the loudest, most uncomfortable dynamics of the grunge era: 'Heart-Shaped Box' and 'All Apologies' became hits, but the record is anchored by darker, stranger songs like 'Scentless Apprentice' and 'Milk It'. When the record label heard Albini's rough mixes, they worried the album had no obvious single, so a few songs, including 'All Apologies', were given gentler remixes, a compromise that frustrated both Cobain and Albini. The result is a record that feels like a scream from inside a person, and its title was sadly prophetic: Cobain died less than a year after it was released.

name: The Velvet Underground & Nico
teaser: 1967 debut — sold about 30,000 copies in its first five years. Brian Eno famously said everyone who bought one started a band. The banana cover was Warhol's idea; early pressings let you peel the banana to reveal a pink fruit underneath.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Sunday Morning' — the celeste that opens it is the same instrument used in every cheesy kids' show for 40 years. The Velvets knew that association and used it deliberately. Then 'Heroin' — Lou Reed's guitar mimics the rush and crash of the drug in real time.

synopsis: The Velvet Underground & Nico (1967) is the album that almost nobody bought when it came out and that almost every band that mattered learned from. Produced and paid for by Andy Warhol, whose banana sticker cover made the record itself a piece of pop art, it took the taboo subjects of the mid-1960s, drug addiction, sadomasochism, prostitution, street violence, and set them to a sound that mixed doo-wop sweetness with a constant, droning noise from John Cale's electric viola and Sterling Morrison's guitar. Lou Reed's lyrics were flat and deadpan, describing the world of Warhol's Factory without judgment, and the German singer Nico, whose voice Warhol insisted on featuring, sang three of the songs, including the hypnotic 'All Tomorrow's Parties'. The band recorded the album in two days of sessions in 1966, but the record label delayed it until March 1967. It sold only a few thousand copies in its first years, but Brian Eno's famous remark that everyone who bought one started a band turned out to be close to the truth. It is now heard as the moment rock music grew up and got dangerous.

name: London Calling
teaser: The Clash 1979 — a double album sold for the price of a single. Recorded in three weeks. The cover photo of Paul Simonon smashing his bass was an accident — Pennie Smith thought it was too blurry to use.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track first — the opening riff is a morse code SOS. Then jump to 'Train in Vain' — it was a last-minute addition, not even listed on the original sleeve. The album spans punk, reggae, rockabilly, and ska in 19 tracks without ever feeling scattered.

synopsis: London Calling (1979) is the double album where punk stopped being a three-chord shout and became capable of anything. The Clash had spent years being told what punk could and could not be, and with this record they answered by throwing in rockabilly, reggae, ska, jazz and R&B, often in the same song. They recorded it at Wessex Studios in London with producer Guy Stevens, who was known for wild behavior in the studio, and the nineteen songs were written quickly and urgently. The title track opens with a walking bassline and a warning about nuclear war, 'The Guns of Brixton' is reggae sung by bassist Paul Simonon, 'Lost in the Supermarket' is a wry look at consumer culture, and 'Train in Vain' was a hidden last track that became a hit single. The cover, a photograph of Simonon smashing his bass guitar on stage in New York, taken by Pennie Smith, is one of the most famous images in rock. It was released as a double album for the price of a single, and Rolling Stone later named it the greatest album of the 1980s.

name: Doolittle
teaser: Pixies 1989 — the quiet-loud-quiet template that Nirvana would borrow wholesale. Black Francis wrote the lyrics on a flight to Los Angeles; the band recorded it in 3 weeks for $40,000. The cover art is a surrealist painting by Simon Larbalestier.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Debaser' — it's about Luis Buñuel's film Un Chien Andalou, specifically the eyeball-slicing scene. Then 'Monkey Gone to Heaven' — count how many times the song switches between quiet and loud. The dynamic whiplash is the point.

synopsis: Doolittle (1989) is the Pixies' second album and the record that showed how much noise and melody could be packed into a pop song. Black Francis wrote most of the songs, drawing on the surreal, the violent and the biblical, and the band's signature was the sudden lurch from a whisper-quiet verse into a screaming chorus, a dynamic shift that Kurt Cobain later admitted he stole outright for Nirvana. The album was recorded in Boston with producer Gil Norton, who helped the band sharpen their sound into something that could still fit on the radio, and it produced their biggest songs: the cryptic 'Monkey Gone to Heaven', about pollution and God, and 'Here Comes Your Man', a bouncy tune the band had been carrying for years. 'Debaser' was inspired by the surrealist film Un Chien Andalou, and its opening scream became a signature. Kim Deal's bass and backing vocals gave the band a warmth that balanced Black Francis's intensity. It sold slowly at first, but its influence on 1990s alternative rock is hard to overstate: nearly every loud-quiet-loud band of the next decade was chasing this record.

name: Automatic for the People
teaser: R.E.M.'s 1992 album — recorded in New Orleans and mostly acoustic. The band deliberately avoided rock songs after the success of 'Out of Time'. Michael Stipe wrote the lyrics in character as an elderly Southern man looking back on his life.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Everybody Hurts' — the string arrangement by John Paul Jones (Led Zeppelin's bassist) was recorded in a single session in Atlanta. Then 'Nightswimming' — just a piano and Stipe's voice, recorded at 3 AM in an empty studio. The album has almost no drums.

synopsis: Automatic for the People (1992) is R.E.M.'s most intimate and melancholy record, made at the peak of their fame. After the aggressive rock of their previous album, Out of Time, they decided to go in the opposite direction, recording mostly acoustic songs with producer Scott Litt at a studio in New Orleans. The album is full of songs about mortality and loss, written in the shadow of deaths in the band members' families and among their friends: the soaring 'Drive', the gospel-tinged 'Man on the Moon' about comedian Andy Kaufman, the devastating 'Everybody Hurts', which drummer Bill Berry wrote after seeing a young person in despair and which became an anthem for people struggling, and 'Nightswimming', a hushed piano song about memories of youth. Michael Stipe's lyrics were more direct and personal than ever before, and Peter Buck's guitar work is subtle and textural rather than flashy. The album sold over four million copies in the US alone and is widely considered their greatest record, proof that a huge band could make a quiet, thoughtful album and have it become their biggest seller.

name: The Joshua Tree
teaser: U2 1987 — recorded in Dublin with Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois. The album was meant to be a love letter to America, inspired by the band's travels through the Mojave Desert. The tree on the cover died in 2000; fans still leave offerings at the site.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Where the Streets Have No Name' — the intro was stitched together from multiple takes because Edge couldn't play the arpeggio cleanly in one go. Then 'I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For' — Bono's vocal was a guide track they couldn't beat, so they kept it.

tracks.title: Where the Streets Have No Name
I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For

synopsis: The Joshua Tree (1987) is the album that made U2 the biggest band in the world. After a tour supporting their experimental record The Unforgettable Fire, the band retreated to Dublin with producers Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois to write songs about a place they had never really known, the American landscape, in all its desert beauty and political violence. Bono had recently traveled to Central America and seen the effects of US foreign policy firsthand, and songs like 'Bullet the Blue Sky' and 'Mothers of the Disappeared' carry that anger. But the album's core is its three monumental singles: 'With or Without You', 'I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For' and 'Where the Streets Have No Name', which open the record with a guitar line that seems to rise out of the desert itself. The band recorded in a house in Dublin and in the American Southwest, and the cover photo, taken in the California desert, shows the four of them small against a vast landscape. It won the Grammy for Album of the Year and sold over twenty-five million copies, turning U2 from a cult band into stadium titans.

name: Unknown Pleasures
teaser: Joy Division 1979 — produced by Martin Hannett for £8,000. Hannett made the drummer Stephen Morris assemble his kit on the roof and miked it from the parking lot. The iconic cover is a plot of radio pulsar CP 1919 from the Cambridge Encyclopedia of Astronomy.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Disorder' — the bassline carries the melody while Ian Curtis's voice floats almost disconnected from the music. Then 'She's Lost Control' — Hannett recorded the drums in a separate room and fed them through a digital delay. The album sounds like a transmission from a cold planet.

synopsis: Unknown Pleasures (1979) is Joy Division's debut album and one of the most influential records of the post-punk era, a bleak and beautiful document of Manchester at the end of the 1970s. Produced by Martin Hannett, who treated the studio as an instrument, the album abandoned the raw punk sound for something colder and more spacious: the drums are distant and echoing, the bass lines are deep and melodic, and Ian Curtis's baritone voice floats above it all, singing lyrics about isolation, anxiety and emotional collapse. Curtis was already suffering from epilepsy, and the song 'She's Lost Control' was inspired by a woman he met at an employment center who had the condition. The band recorded the album in three days of sessions, but Hannett spent weeks mixing it, layering in strange sounds and silences. The cover, a series of white pulses on black, is a print of radio waves from a pulsar, designed by Peter Saville without even telling the band what the image was. Released on the tiny Factory label, it sold steadily and became a cult classic; Curtis died by suicide in May 1980, less than a year later, and the album's cold beauty only grew in legend.

name: The Queen Is Dead
teaser: The Smiths 1986 — Johnny Marr wrote all the music in a creative burst over a few weeks. Morrissey's lyrics cycle through despair, wit, and melancholic nostalgia. The title track was recorded in a single take with Morrissey improvising much of the vocal.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'There Is a Light That Never Goes Out' — the strings were lifted from a 1960s film score. Johnny Marr played them himself on a Roland guitar synthesizer. Then 'I Know It's Over' — Morrissey recorded the vocal lying on the studio floor in near-darkness.

tracks.title: The Boy with the Thorn in His Side
There Is a Light That Never Goes Out
Some Girls Are Bigger Than Others

synopsis: The Queen Is Dead (1986) is The Smiths' masterpiece, the album where Johnny Marr's guitar and Morrissey's words reached their full power together. The title is a joke aimed at both the monarchy and the band Queen, and the record is full of the band's signature mix of wit and melancholy. Marr wrote the music in an intense burst of creativity, layering ringing, jangling guitars that sounded like no one else at the time, while Morrissey's lyrics moved from savage social satire to tender longing, sometimes in the same song: 'Bigmouth Strikes Again' is a self-mocking scream about putting your foot in it, 'The Boy with the Thorn in His Side' is about the pain of being misunderstood, and the closing 'There Is a Light That Never Goes Out', with its famous line about dying in the back of someone's car, became the band's signature anthem. The band recorded the album in London and Manchester, and it was released to ecstatic reviews. It is the record on which The Smiths stopped being an indie cult and became the most beloved British band of their generation, and it has never gone out of print.

name: In Rainbows
teaser: Radiohead 2007 — self-released as a pay-what-you-want download, a first for a major band. The album was recorded in a crumbling country house in Oxfordshire over two years. The band lived and cooked together; the domestic warmth seeps into every track.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Weird Fishes/Arpeggi' — the guitar loop was built by layering single notes, each recorded separately. Then 'Reckoner' — the falsetto vocal was a late addition; Thom Yorke improvised it over an instrumental track the band thought was finished.

synopsis: In Rainbows (2007) is the album Radiohead released on their own terms, famously as a pay-what-you-want download, and it turned out to be their warmest and most human record in years. After the dense electronic experiments of Kid A and Amnesiac and the difficult sessions for Hail to the Thief, the band went back to playing together in a room, recording over many months in their own studio and a converted barn in Oxfordshire, often improvising and jamming until songs emerged. The result is an album built on texture and rhythm: the nervous guitar of '15 Step' with its odd time signature, the interlocking guitars of 'Weird Fishes/Arpeggi', the lush 'Nude', which they had been trying to record for a decade, and the motorik pulse of 'Bodysnatchers'. Yorke's lyrics are more romantic and less paranoid than before, songs about love, insecurity and connection. The pay-what-you-want release was a gamble that became a landmark moment for the music industry, and the album itself was greeted as a return to form, winning the Grammy for Best Alternative Album and selling out its physical edition within days.

name: AM
teaser: Arctic Monkeys 2013 — recorded in Joshua Tree at Rancho De La Luna, a studio built into a desert house. Alex Turner wrote the lyrics on a BlackBerry. The album blends heavy riffs with R&B-influenced grooves inspired by Aaliyah and Dr. Dre.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Do I Wanna Know?' — the riff was built from a single drum machine loop slowed way down. Then 'Arabella' — Turner's guitar solo references War Pigs by Black Sabbath, but played through a fuzz pedal at half-speed. The whole album sounds like 2 AM in a leather jacket.

tracks.title: Why'd You Only Call Me When You're High?

synopsis: AM (2013) is the album where Arctic Monkeys stopped being a British indie band and became a global rock band, built on a sound that owed as much to hip-hop and 1970s rock as to their Sheffield garage roots. Alex Turner wrote much of it in Los Angeles, and the record's mood is late-night and confident: heavy, slow-burning grooves, tight falsetto backing vocals and lyrics full of one-liners about modern romance. The band recorded in California with producer James Ford and in their home city, and the album's centerpiece 'Do I Wanna Know?' became their biggest hit, its huge, distorted opening riff impossible to escape in 2013. 'R U Mine?' had already won them a Brit Award the year before, and the album also contains the sweet 'Arabella', the ominous 'Why'd You Only Call Me When You're High?' and a cover of a John Cooper Clarke poem set to music, 'I Wanna Be Yours'. The record went to number one on both sides of the Atlantic, and its minimal cover art, just the band name in a simple font, became one of the most imitated designs of the decade.

name: Rumours
teaser: Fleetwood Mac 1977 — recorded while both couples in the band (John & Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham & Stevie Nicks) were breaking up. The studio was a war zone. They channeled the pain into perfect California pop. It's sold over 40 million copies.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Go Your Own Way' and 'Dreams' back to back — they're Buckingham and Nicks answering each other across the same breakup. Then 'The Chain' — the only song credited to all five members, and the bassline at 3:05 is John McVie's one-take improvisation.

synopsis: Rumours (1977) is one of the best-selling albums of all time, and the reason it sounds the way it does is that the band was falling apart while they made it. By the time Fleetwood Mac went into the studio in 1976, both of the album's couples, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks, and Christine and John McVie, were breaking up, and the band channelled all of that pain and anger into the songs. Buckingham wrote 'Go Your Own Way' as a direct message to Nicks, who answered with 'Dreams', the album's only number one single, while Christine McVie contributed 'Don't Stop' and 'You Make Loving Fun', and the band assembled 'The Chain' from leftover fragments of other songs, making it a symbol of their tangled relationships. They recorded at studios in Sausalito and Los Angeles with producers Ken Caillat and Richard Dashut, often working through the night amid the chaos of their personal lives. The result is an album that sounds effortless, full of gorgeous harmonies and hooks, yet is about heartbreak on every track. It won the Grammy for Album of the Year and has sold over forty million copies, one of the most durable records of the 1970s.

name: Hotel California
teaser: Eagles 1976 — recorded over eight months in three different studios. The title track's famous guitar duel between Don Felder and Joe Walsh was planned note-for-note, not improvised. The album was the last with original bassist Randy Meisner.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track on headphones — the guitar harmonies at the end were triple-tracked with different EQ settings to create the illusion of more players. Then 'Life in the Fast Lane' — the opening riff was a warm-up exercise Joe Walsh played that Glenn Frey insisted they use.

tracks.title: Pretty Maids All in a Row

synopsis: Hotel California (1976) is the Eagles' dark masterpiece, the album where the band of sunny California rock turned its gaze on the corruption and excess of the life they were living. The title track became one of the most famous songs in rock history: a narrator checks into a beautiful hotel that turns out to be a trap, and the lyrics have been read as an allegory about hedonism, addiction and the music business itself. The song's centerpiece is its long, intertwining guitar duel between Don Felder and Joe Walsh, played live in the studio, that has become one of the most beloved solos ever recorded. The album was made over eight months in three different studios, with producer Bill Szymczyk, and it also contains the driving 'New Kid in Town', the ballad 'Wasted Time' and the menacing 'Life in the Fast Lane'. It sold over sixteen million copies in the US alone and won the Grammy for Record of the Year for the title track. It stands as the moment the Eagles went from hitmakers to one of the defining American rock bands of the decade.

name: Born to Run
teaser: Bruce Springsteen 1975 — recorded over 14 months at the Record Plant in New York. Springsteen was 25 and obsessed with Phil Spector's Wall of Sound. He recorded dozens of guitar overdubs, layering them until the album sounded like it was bursting out of the speakers.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the glockenspiel in the opening is played by Springsteen himself. The saxophone solo by Clarence Clemons was recorded in one take at 3 AM. The entire album is designed to sound like a car radio at full volume on a summer night.

synopsis: Born to Run (1975) is the album where Bruce Springsteen went from cult hero to the man the critics called the future of rock and roll. He spent months writing and recording it, trying to capture the sound of Phil Spector's wall of sound with a rock band, and the songs are about getting out of a dead-end town, engines running, headlights on the highway. The title track opens with one of the most famous drum-and-guitar intros in rock, and its story of a young couple fleeing into the night became the blueprint for everything Springsteen did after. 'Thunder Road' is the opening statement, a whispered invitation to escape; 'Backstreets' and 'Jungleland' are longer, darker tales of the same streets, and the album closes with 'Jungleland', a ten-minute epic with a saxophone solo by Clarence Clemons that sounds like the city itself. Recorded in New York with the E Street Band, it was released in August 1975, and Springsteen appeared on the covers of Time and Newsweek in the same week, a level of hype few artists had ever faced. The album delivered on it, and it remains the definitive record of American youth and restlessness.

name: Remain in Light
teaser: Talking Heads 1980 — recorded in the Bahamas and New York with Brian Eno. The band built the songs from layered loops, inspired by Fela Kuti's Afrobeat. David Byrne wrote the lyrics by improvising nonsense syllables over the grooves, then shaping words around the sounds.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Once in a Lifetime' — Byrne's sermon-like vocal was inspired by a recording of a preacher he found on the radio. The bassline by Tina Weymouth cycles through the same figure for the entire song without ever becoming boring. Then 'The Great Curve' — six guitar parts woven into one.

tracks.title: Born Under Punches (The Heat Goes On)

synopsis: Remain in Light (1980) is the album where Talking Heads stopped being a quirky New York art-rock band and became something else entirely, a machine built from rhythm. Working again with producer Brian Eno, the band started with drummer Chris Frantz and bassist Tina Weymouth laying down deep, repeating grooves, then layered guitars, keyboards and percussion on top, inspired by the polyrhythms of the Afrobeat music of Fela Kuti that Eno had been playing for them. David Byrne's vocals were built from fragments of improvised spoken word, cut up and rearranged into lyrics that drift through consciousness like thoughts: the paranoid monologue of 'Once in a Lifetime', with its famous refrain asking if you are really who you think you are, and the ecstatic 'The Great Curve'. The band expanded to include extra musicians, including keyboardist Bernie Worrell and guitarist Adrian Belew, and the record's dense, interlocking sound was unlike anything they had made before. It was hailed as a masterpiece on release and remains one of the most influential albums of the 1980s, the moment rock music absorbed African rhythm and funk into something new.

name: Pet Sounds
teaser: The Beach Boys 1966 — Brian Wilson at 23, listening to Rubber Soul on repeat, paying session musicians to realize everything he heard in his head. He used bicycle horns, sleigh bells, Coca-Cola cans, and a theremin. Capitol Records almost refused to release it.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'God Only Knows' — Paul McCartney called it the most perfect song ever written. Carl Wilson was 19 when he sang it; Brian picked him because his voice had less vibrato. The album uses a 12-string bass that Wilson had custom-made because he wanted a sound between guitar and bass.

tracks.title: Don't Talk (Put Your Head on My Shoulder)
I Just Wasn't Made for These Times

synopsis: Pet Sounds (1966) is Brian Wilson's attempt to answer the Beatles' Rubber Soul, and in the process he created one of the most influential albums ever made. Wilson had stopped touring with the Beach Boys to focus on writing and producing, and he filled the album with instruments pop records had never used together: sleigh bells, bicycle bells, timpani, flutes, French horns, harpsichord and a full string section, arranged into elaborate vocal harmonies over song structures far more complex than pop was supposed to allow. The lyrics, mostly written with Tony Asher, are about longing, loneliness and the ache of love, and they matched the music's melancholy beauty: 'Wouldn't It Be Nice' is a teenager's fantasy of growing up, 'God Only Knows', which Paul McCartney called the greatest song ever written, is a love song that admits the possibility of loss, and the closing 'Caroline, No' is a heartbreaking song about the passage of time. The album was recorded with Los Angeles session musicians known as the Wrecking Crew while the rest of the band was on tour, which caused lasting tension. It sold poorly in the US at first but became a landmark, influencing the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper and every ambitious pop record after it.

name: The Stone Roses
teaser: The Stone Roses 1989 — the album that launched the Madchester scene and made baggy clothes and dance-rock a thing. John Squire was inspired by Jackson Pollock for the cover art; he splattered paint on a canvas and photographed it in his kitchen.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'I Wanna Be Adored' — the intro builds for nearly two minutes before a word is sung. The bassline never changes but the guitar layers accumulate until the song feels submerged. Then 'Fools Gold' — a 9-minute funk groove built from a James Brown sample played backwards.

synopsis: The Stone Roses' debut album (1989) is the record that kicked off the Madchester scene and gave British indie music its own summer of love. The band had spent years gigging in Manchester, and the album, recorded in the studio with producer John Leckie, captured their sound at its peak: John Squire's chiming, psychedelic guitar lines, Mani's driving bass, Reni's loose, funky drumming and Ian Brown's detached, sung-spoken vocals. Songs like 'I Wanna Be Adored', which builds for nearly two minutes before the band even comes in, 'She Bangs the Drums' and 'Waterfall' became anthems, mixing the swagger of the Rolling Stones with the euphoria of dance music. The cover art, a painting by Squire inspired by Jackson Pollock, became nearly as famous as the music. The band's record label released it with little fanfare and it took over a year to find an audience, but when it did, it transformed British music, and the album is now regarded as one of the greatest debut records of all time. The band's refusal to capitalize on their success, including turning down huge American offers, became part of their legend.

name: The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars
teaser: David Bowie 1972 — recorded in just two weeks at Trident Studios. Bowie created the Ziggy character and wrote the entire album in character as an androgynous alien rock star. Mick Ronson's string arrangements were his first ever — he learned arranging by watching a BBC documentary.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Five Years' — the song builds from a single drumbeat to a full-band apocalypse. Bowie's vocal cracks are deliberate; he wanted to sound like he was on the edge of crying. Then 'Starman' — Bowie sings the chorus an octave above the verse, a move that made the song feel like it was taking off.

synopsis: The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars (1972) is the album where David Bowie invented a character and then lived inside it. Ziggy Stardust is an alien rock star who comes to Earth to deliver a message of hope before the world ends, and Bowie wrote the album as a loose concept record telling his story, while also making space for standalone classics. Recorded in just two weeks at Trident Studios in London with producer Ken Scott and guitarist Mick Ronson, whose arrangements gave the album its theatrical grandeur, it was released at the peak of the glam rock movement. Songs like 'Starman', with its call to the youth of Earth, 'Moonage Daydream' and the frantic 'Suffragette City' became hits, and the title track is a five-minute rock opera about the price of fame. Bowie appeared on Top of the Pops in a multicolored jumpsuit and makeup, an image that terrified and thrilled Britain in equal measure, and the character became so consuming that he eventually had to kill Ziggy off on stage in 1973. The album made him a star and remains one of the most influential rock records ever made.

name: Funeral
teaser: Arcade Fire 2004 — recorded in an old church in Montreal over a single winter. The band used the natural reverb of the space instead of studio effects. Several band members had recently lost family members, hence the title; the album is a wake that turns into a celebration.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Neighborhood #1 (Tunnels)' — the opening piano was recorded in the church's sanctuary at 2 AM. Then 'Wake Up' — the choir singing the wordless chorus was the band and their friends, all crowded around one microphone. The album feels like it was recorded by a much larger group than six people.

synopsis: Funeral (2004) is the debut album that made Arcade Fire the most important new band of the mid-2000s. The title came from a string of deaths in the band members' families during the recording, and the album is full of grief, but also of the desperate joy of being alive. Win Butler, Régine Chassagne and their ever-growing collective of friends recorded in a small studio in an old church in Montreal, and the building's natural reverb shaped the album's huge, echoing sound, which they built from strings, accordion, violins and layers of voices. The songs are grand and anthemic but never simple: 'Neighborhood #1 (Tunnels)' imagines two lovers tunneling through the snow to escape their parents, 'Wake Up' is a shout of defiance that became a festival anthem, and 'Rebellion (Lies)' is a song about refusing to accept what you are told. The band recorded the album on a small budget and released it to little fanfare, but word spread quickly, and it ended up on countless year-end lists and helped define the sound of indie rock for years. It is an album about death that somehow feels completely alive.

name: Exile on Main St.
teaser: The Rolling Stones 1972 — recorded in the basement of Keith Richards' rented villa in the South of France while the band was fleeing UK tax authorities. The sessions were chaos: musicians came and went at all hours, drug dealers doubled as roadies, and the electricity kept cutting out.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Tumbling Dice' — the backing vocals by Merry Clayton and Clydie King were recorded at 3 AM after they'd been woken up to sing. Then 'Shine a Light' — Mick Jagger's vocal was recorded in a tiny bathroom for natural reverb. The album sounds like a radio station broadcasting from a house party you weren't invited to.

tracks.title: I Just Want to See His Face

synopsis: Exile on Main St. (1972) is the Rolling Stones at their most ragged and most brilliant, a double album recorded in the chaos of the band fleeing Britain for tax reasons and setting up in a villa in the south of France. They converted the basement of Keith Richards' rented house, Villa Nellcôte, into a studio using the Rolling Stones Mobile, and recorded late into the night whenever the mood struck, with an ever-changing cast of musicians dropping in. The result is loose, sweaty and deeply American, steeped in blues, gospel, country and swamp rock: 'Rocks Off' opens the album with a horn blast, 'Tumbling Dice' became a hit single about a gambler, 'Sweet Virginia' and 'Torn and Frayed' are country songs, and 'Let It Loose' is a gospel-inflected epic. Jagger's vocals were often recorded in a makeshift booth, and the album has a murky, lived-in sound that critics initially found muddy and fans came to adore. It topped charts on both sides of the Atlantic and is now widely regarded as the band's greatest album, the sound of a rock and roll band at the absolute peak of its powers, captured at its most natural.

name: Sticky Fingers
teaser: The Rolling Stones 1971 — the first album on their own label, with the famous Andy Warhol zipper cover that damaged adjacent records in shipping. Recorded partly at Muscle Shoals in Alabama, partly at Mick Jagger's country house. The opening riff of 'Brown Sugar' was written by Jagger in 45 minutes during a film shoot.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Wild Horses' — Keith Richards wrote the chorus while sitting in a bathroom, feeling guilty about leaving his newborn son to go on tour. Then 'Can't You Hear Me Knocking' — the jam at the end was an accident; the band thought the song was over and kept playing. The tape was still rolling.

synopsis: Sticky Fingers (1971) is the album where the Rolling Stones, after years of being managed by others, finally took control of their own career, releasing it on their own label. It also has one of the most famous album covers in history: Andy Warhol's close-up of a man's crotch in tight jeans, with a working zipper that opens to reveal underwear, a design that caused no end of trouble for record stores and damaged records as they stacked them. The music is the Stones at their peak, mixing the country sweetness of 'Wild Horses', written about the end of a relationship and recorded with a gospel choir, the swaggering 'Brown Sugar', the raunchy 'Bitch' and the paranoid 'Can't You Hear Me Knocking', whose long instrumental coda became legendary. Recorded at Muscle Shoals Sound Studio in Alabama and in London, with producer Jimmy Miller, it was the first album to feature Mick Taylor fully, and his fluid guitar work is all over it. The album was a huge hit and is regarded as one of the great runs of records the Stones made between 1968 and 1972, the sound of a band that could do anything.

name: Who's Next
teaser: The Who 1971 — salvaged from Pete Townshend's abandoned 'Lifehouse' project, a sci-fi rock opera he never finished. The songs were rescued and re-recorded with producer Glyn Johns. The famous synth loop on 'Baba O'Riley' was Townshend's Lowrey organ fed through a VCS3 synthesizer, programmed to cycle forever.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Baba O'Riley' — the violin solo at the end is Dave Arbus of East of Eden, recorded in one take. Then 'Behind Blue Eyes' — Townshend wrote it after a show when he felt like the audience wanted the rock star, not the person. The song shifts from ballad to full-band assault in the bridge.

synopsis: Who's Next (1971) is the album the Who made after their grand rock opera Lifehouse collapsed, and the songs that survived became their greatest record. Pete Townshend had spent two years trying to build Lifehouse, a multimedia science-fiction project about a world without music where a young man's guitar playing could save humanity, and when it became clear it would never work, the band took the best songs and recorded them as a straightforward album. The result is a collection of towering rock songs built on Townshend's new obsession with synthesizers: 'Baba O'Riley' opens with a keyboard loop that sounds like a computer waking up, named after his guru Meher Baba and minimalist composer Terry Riley, 'Bargain' is a ferocious rocker, and 'Won't Get Fooled Again' ends with one of the most famous drum breaks in rock, Keith Moon's wild solo at the close. The album also contains 'Behind Blue Eyes', a ballad sung from the point of view of a villain, and the gentle 'The Song Is Over'. Recorded in London and New York with producer Glyn Johns, it became the Who's best-selling album and the template for the stadium rock they would pioneer for the rest of the decade.

name: Are You Experienced
teaser: Jimi Hendrix 1967 — the debut that rewired what electric guitar could sound like. Hendrix was 24, had been in the US Army, and had backed Little Richard and the Isley Brothers. He recorded the album in London with a mostly British rhythm section who couldn't believe what they were hearing.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Purple Haze' — the famous opening riff came to Hendrix in a dream. The solo was recorded in two passes, panned hard left and right. Then 'Third Stone from the Sun' — Hendrix slows down his guitar to sound like a cello, then a spaceship. He told the engineer to leave the mistakes in because 'mistakes are just notes that didn't know where they were going.'

synopsis: Are You Experienced (1967) is the debut album that rewired the electric guitar. Jimi Hendrix arrived in London in late 1966 as a little-known American guitarist who had backed the Isley Brothers and Little Richard, and within months he had formed the Jimi Hendrix Experience with bassist Noel Redding and drummer Mitch Mitchell and become the most talked-about musician in Britain. The album was recorded quickly in London and captures the sound that made him famous: songs built on huge, distorted riffs, with wah-wah, feedback and all the new effects he was pioneering, played with a freedom nobody had heard. 'Purple Haze' opens with a dissonant, unforgettable riff, 'Foxy Lady' is pure swagger, 'The Wind Cries Mary' is a tender ballad inspired by his girlfriend, and 'Hey Joe', a cover of a folk song, became his first hit. Hendrix could play blues, R&B and noise all at once, and the album's title track asks the listener, almost tauntingly, whether they are ready for what they are hearing. It reached number two in Britain and was released in the US later that year, where it went to the top of the charts and changed rock music forever.

name: The Doors
teaser: The Doors 1967 — recorded in 6 days at Sunset Sound in Hollywood for $10,000. Jim Morrison was so nervous about his voice that he recorded many of the vocals in the control room with the lights off. The album ends with 'The End', an 11-minute Oedipal nightmare they'd been kicked off stage for playing live.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Light My Fire' — the extended organ and guitar solos were edited down from a 7-minute jam. Robby Krieger wrote the melody; it was his first song. Then 'The End' — Morrison's vocal was recorded in one continuous take, and you can hear a door creak open at 4:22 that they decided to leave in.

tracks.title: Break On Through (To the Other Side)

synopsis: The Doors' debut album (1967) introduced one of the most theatrical and dangerous bands rock had produced, and it still sounds like a warning. The band, keyboardist Ray Manzarek, guitarist Robby Krieger, drummer John Densmore and singer Jim Morrison, had no bass player; Manzarek played the bass lines with his left hand on the keyboard, which gave their sound its dark, hypnotic quality. Morrison was a poetry student who sang like he was possessed, and the album's songs move from the driving 'Break On Through (To the Other Side)' to the seductive 'Light My Fire', which became their first number one single, and the eleven-minute 'The End', an Oedipal epic with the famous line about killing your father and fucking your mother, recorded in the studio after they had only ever performed it live. The band recorded the album quickly in Los Angeles, and it became one of the most successful debuts of the decade. Morrison's image as the shamanic Lizard King was born here, and the album's mix of poetry, blues, jazz and menace made the Doors seem like they were playing from somewhere darker than the Sunset Strip.

name: Disraeli Gears
teaser: Cream 1967 — the first supergroup (Clapton, Bruce, Baker) recorded their second album in 3 days at Atlantic Studios in New York, fueled by psychedelics and sleeplessness. The album cover was designed by Australian artist Martin Sharp, who lived with Clapton in a Chelsea flat that became a psychedelic crash pad.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Sunshine of Your Love' — the riff was inspired by a Jimi Hendrix show. Bruce adapted the lyric from a poem by friend Pete Brown. Then 'Tales of Brave Ulysses' — Clapton used a wah-wah pedal for the first time, having borrowed it from Hendrix. The song's lyric was written on a napkin at a Greek restaurant.

synopsis: Disraeli Gears (1967) is the album where Cream, the first supergroup, went from blues purists to psychedelic pioneers. Eric Clapton, Jack Bruce and Ginger Baker had formed the band the year before as a showcase for Clapton's blues guitar, but by their second album they were experimenting with the sounds of 1967: wah-wah pedals, fuzz, harmonies and studio effects. The title is a mistake: the band misheard a phrase from a British blues song and thought it sounded good. Recorded in just three days in New York with producer Felix Pappalardi, the album contains some of the most enduring songs of the era: 'Sunshine of Your Love', whose riff became one of the most recognizable in rock, 'Tales of Brave Ulysses', with its wah-wah guitar and lyrics about the Trojan War, and 'Strange Brew', which opens the album. The cover, a swirling collage of colors with a photo of the band, became an icon of psychedelic design. The album made Cream superstars and is the record that showed how blues, when played at full volume with virtuoso musicians, could become hard rock.

name: Harvest
teaser: Neil Young 1972 — recorded mostly in a barn in rural California with an ad-hoc band called the Stray Gators. The London Symphony Orchestra appeared on two tracks. 'Heart of Gold' became his only #1 single. Young later said the album 'put me in the middle of the road' and deliberately made darker music to escape it.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Heart of Gold' — James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt sing backing vocals. The harmonica parts were recorded in a separate session in Nashville. Then 'The Needle and the Damage Done' — recorded live at UCLA, a stark solo acoustic performance about friends lost to heroin. The audience doesn't clap at the end.

tracks.title: Are You Ready for the Country?
The Needle and the Damage Done

synopsis: Harvest (1972) is the album that made Neil Young a star, and it remains his most beloved record. After years of making ragged, uncompromising music with Crazy Horse, Young suddenly found himself with a huge hit on his hands, and the album is full of the gentlest, most direct songs he ever wrote. It was recorded in Nashville with a group of country session musicians, in London with the London Symphony Orchestra on 'A Man Needs a Maid', and in a barn on his ranch in California with an ad-hoc band he called the Stray Gators. The centerpiece is 'Heart of Gold', the song Young later said put him in the middle of the road, with its simple harmonica and vocal line, and which became his only number one single. The album also contains 'Old Man', written about the caretaker of his ranch, and 'The Needle and the Damage Done', a stark warning about drug addiction written about friends he had lost, including Crazy Horse guitarist Danny Whitten, who died of an overdose shortly after. It topped the charts in the US and UK, and Young, uncomfortable with the fame, responded by recording the deliberately difficult Tonight's the Night, which he held back for years.

name: Tonight's the Night
teaser: Neil Young 1975 — recorded as a raw wake for roadie Bruce Berry and Crazy Horse guitarist Danny Whitten, both dead from heroin overdoses. Young played the album for his label's executives; they asked where the 'real' album was. He shelved it for two years before releasing it unchanged.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — Young's voice cracks on the first word and never recovers. The whole album was recorded in a single studio with the lights dimmed and the air thick with tequila and grief. Nils Lofgren plays piano on several tracks while crying. No album sounds more like a wake.

tracks.title: Come On Baby Let's Go Downtown

synopsis: Tonight's the Night (1975) is Neil Young's rawest record, an album of grief so personal that he sat on it for two years before releasing it. In 1973, two people close to him died within months: roadie Bruce Berry and Crazy Horse guitarist Danny Whitten, both from drug-related deaths. Young responded by going into the studio with a new band and recording a set of ragged, drunken-sounding songs that felt like a wake, full of loose playing, slurred vocals and dark humor. The title track is a slow, druggy blues about Berry, 'Tired Eyes' tells a story of murder and cocaine in a detached mumble, and 'Lookout Joe' and 'New Mama' are fragments of life and death set to music. He recorded most of it live in the studio in a few days, often with friends drinking along, and the result sounds like a party at the end of the world. When he finally released it, many fans and critics were confused by its roughness, but it has since been recognized as one of his greatest records, a honest portrait of loss that made the polished singer-songwriter confessions of the era sound like lies.

name: Horses
teaser: Patti Smith 1975 — recorded at Electric Lady Studios, the studio built for Jimi Hendrix who died before it was finished. Smith opened the album with 'Jesus died for somebody's sins but not mine', a line that made John Cale (her producer, from the Velvet Underground) know he was working with something dangerous.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Gloria' — Smith transforms Van Morrison's garage-rock classic into a feminist manifesto in the opening monologue. Then 'Birdland' — inspired by a Peter Reich memoir about his father Wilhelm Reich, the controversial psychoanalyst. Smith recorded the vocal reading from the book.

synopsis: Horses (1975) is the album that connected poetry to punk before punk existed. Patti Smith was a New York poet who had been performing with guitarist Lenny Kaye at rock readings, and when she finally made an album, produced by John Cale of the Velvet Underground, she brought a poet's language to the raw energy of garage rock. The album opens with a cover of the Them song 'Gloria', which she rewrites into a poem about a girl who wants to be a star, and it closes with the eleven-minute 'Land', a hallucinatory epic about a boy named Johnny who is attacked in an alley and finds himself flying through the air. In between are songs like 'Birdland', based on a science fiction novel about a man who travels to meet his dead mother, and 'Break It Up', written with Tom Verlaine. The cover photo, taken by Robert Mapplethorpe, shows Smith in a white shirt with a jacket slung over her shoulder, and became as iconic as the music. The album was released months before the Ramones and the Sex Pistols, and it is now heard as one of the founding documents of punk, proof that rock could be intellectual and visceral at the same time.

name: Ramones
teaser: Ramones 1976 — 14 songs in 29 minutes, recorded in 7 days for $6,400. The fastest, simplest rock album ever made. Johnny Ramone played every downstroke as hard as he could; Tommy played the drums standing up because his stool broke. The album invented punk rock while selling only 6,000 copies in its first year.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Blitzkrieg Bop' — the 'Hey ho, let's go' chant was Tommy's idea, borrowed from the Bay City Rollers. Every song on the album has the same tempo: fast. Then 'I Wanna Be Your Boyfriend' — the slowest track at a relatively leisurely 3 minutes. The Ramones claimed they were just a bubblegum pop band playing too fast.

tracks.title: Now I Wanna Sniff Some Glue
I Don't Wanna Go Down to the Basement
I Don't Wanna Walk Around with You
Today Your Love, Tomorrow the World
I Don't Wanna Be Learned/I Don't Wanna Be Tamed
You Should Never Have Opened That Door

synopsis: The Ramones' self-titled debut (1976) is the album that invented punk rock, even if nobody called it that yet. Four friends from Queens, New York, had decided to start a band that played faster, louder and dumber than anything around them, and their first album contains fourteen songs in under thirty minutes, none of them longer than three chords and a shout. The songs are about boredom, girls, glue sniffing, beatings and rock and roll itself: 'Blitzkrieg Bop' with its 'hey ho, let's go' chant, 'Beat on the Brat', 'Now I Wanna Sniff Some Glue' and 'I Don't Wanna Go Down to the Basement'. They recorded the album in a week for a tiny budget at a studio in New York, and the production, by Craig Leon, gave the songs a flat, garage sound that perfectly matched their aesthetic. The band wore leather jackets and torn jeans and posed for the cover like a street gang. It sold almost nothing at first, but when the album reached Britain a year later, it lit a fire under the nascent punk scene, and nearly every punk band that followed, from the Clash to the Sex Pistols to Nirvana, owed something to these fourteen songs.

name: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols
teaser: Sex Pistols 1977 — the only studio album from the band that terrified the British establishment. The title got them taken to court for obscenity (they won). Recorded over several chaotic sessions with producers being fired mid-album. The band couldn't really play their instruments, which was the point.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'God Save the Queen' — released during the Queen's Silver Jubilee, the BBC banned it. It still reached #2 on the charts (many believe it was #1 but kept off for political reasons). Then 'Anarchy in the UK' — Johnny Rotten's sneer was real; he'd been rejected by every school and employer in London.

synopsis: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols (1977) is the only studio album the Sex Pistols ever made, and it is still the most confrontational record in British rock. Released at the height of the punk explosion, with a title that got it banned from major retailers and its cover, a ransom-note collage of letters, became a design classic. The songs are short, fast and furious, built on Steve Jones's wall of guitar and Johnny Rotten's snarling, sarcastic vocals: 'Anarchy in the U.K.' is a manifesto against everything, 'God Save the Queen' attacked the monarchy so directly that the BBC banned it and it still sold over 150,000 copies in a week, and 'Pretty Vacant' and 'Holidays in the Sun' complete the set. The band recorded the album over many months with producer Chris Thomas, and by the time it came out they were already falling apart, with bassist Sid Vicious having replaced Glen Matlock. It was released in October 1977 and immediately became a landmark, the sound of a generation that felt it had nothing to lose. The Sex Pistols imploded within months, but the album has never stopped being essential.

name: Singles Going Steady
teaser: Buzzcocks 1979 — a compilation of 8 UK singles that became the template for pop-punk. Pete Shelley wrote songs about unrequited love, sexual confusion, and boredom over three-chord guitar rushes that rarely passed the 2:30 mark. The album is a singles band proving the singles format is the point, not the limitation.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Ever Fallen in Love (With Someone You Shouldn't've)' — Shelley wrote it about a man he was in love with while still publicly closeted. Then 'What Do I Get?' — the question is genuinely asked, not rhetorical. The Buzzcocks made punk that admitted vulnerability instead of hiding behind aggression.

tracks.title: Ever Fallen in Love (With Someone You Shouldn't've)
You Say You Don't Love Me
Why She's a Girl from the Chainstore

synopsis: Singles Going Steady (1979) is the album that defined pop punk, even though it is technically a collection of singles. Buzzcocks had been releasing a string of perfect three-minute pop songs on their own label since 1977, and this compilation gathered them together: 'What Do I Get?', 'Ever Fallen in Love (With Someone You Shouldn't've)?', 'Orgasm Addict', 'Autonomy' and the rest. Pete Shelley wrote songs about unrequited love, sexual confusion and emotional awkwardness with a tunefulness that most punk bands refused to admit they had, while Steve Diggle's songs added a tougher edge. The band's sound mixed the speed and anger of punk with the craftsmanship of the Beatles and the Kinks, and the result was music that could make you dance and break your heart in the same verse. The album became a template: every pop punk band from Green Day to the Descendents learned their craft from these twelve songs. It remains the definitive document of a band that proved punk could be melodic without losing its bite.

name: Entertainment!
teaser: Gang of Four 1979 — Marxist theory set to funk-punk rhythms. Andy Gill's guitar playing was described by one critic as sounding like 'a dentist's drill attacking sheet metal'. The band was named after the Chinese Communist Party leaders arrested during the Cultural Revolution.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Damaged Goods' — the bassline by Dave Allen is a funk groove played by someone who learned bass last week. Then 'Anthrax' — two vocalists sing completely different lyrics simultaneously: one a love song, the other an essay about why love songs are ideologically suspect. The album influenced R.E.M., Red Hot Chili Peppers, and Franz Ferdinand equally.

synopsis: Entertainment! (1979) is the album that married radical politics to danceable funk and invented a whole strain of post-punk in the process. Gang of Four were four art students from Leeds who had read Marxist theory and decided that rock music, which they saw as a tool of capitalist alienation, needed to be dismantled from the inside. The result was a record of tense, fractured funk: Andy Gill's guitar stabbed and stuttered instead of strumming, bassist Dave Allen played locked, syncopated grooves, and singer Jon King shouted and sermonized about the commodity of love, the tyranny of work and the violence hiding in everyday life. 'Damaged Goods' and 'At Home He's a Tourist' are the best-known tracks, but the whole album works as a single furious argument. It had a huge influence on bands who came later, from the Red Hot Chili Peppers, whose bassist cited it constantly, to Rage Against the Machine and countless post-punk revivalists. Few debut albums have ever sounded so intellectually angry and so physically irresistible at the same time.

name: Pink Flag
teaser: Wire 1977 — 21 songs in 35 minutes, none longer than 4 minutes. The album reduces punk to its atomic components: a riff, a verse, a chorus, stop. Producer Mike Thorne insisted on clean recording quality when every other punk band wanted distortion, making the album sound even more alien and precise.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Three Girl Rhumba' — the entire song is one riff played 66 times with five words of lyric. Elastica were later sued for basing 'Connection' on it. Then 'Reuters' — the opening track that sounds nothing like the rest of the album: a slow-building drone while a BBC news broadcast plays in the background.

synopsis: Pink Flag (1977) is the most radical debut album of the punk era, a record that stripped rock down to nothing and then reassembled it as a series of sparks. Wire were art school students who approached punk as an intellectual exercise, and their first album contains twenty-one songs in thirty-five minutes, none longer than three and a half minutes and many under a minute. Songs like 'Three Girl Rhumba' and 'Ex Lion Tamer' were built on strange, angular riffs rather than the standard three-chord patterns of their punk peers, and the whole record had a cold, cryptic quality that made it feel less like rebellion and more like an alien transmission. The band were so far ahead of the scene that when the album was released, many punk fans did not know what to make of it, and the group moved on to increasingly experimental territory with their next album Chairs Missing. Decades later, the album's influence can be heard everywhere, from hardcore to post-punk to alternative rock, and it is rightly regarded as one of the most important records of the 1970s.

name: Disintegration
teaser: The Cure 1989 — Robert Smith was turning 30 and terrified of becoming irrelevant. He locked himself in his room and wrote the darkest album of his career. The band nearly broke up during recording; Lol Tolhurst was fired for alcoholism mid-session. Smith later said the album saved his life.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Pictures of You' — the opening guitar line was inspired by a fire that destroyed Smith's childhood home; photographs were among the only things he saved. Then 'Lullaby' — the spider-creature is a metaphor for Smith's depression. The album was mixed on headphones, making it sound enormous and claustrophobic simultaneously.

tracks.title: The Same Deep Water as You

synopsis: Disintegration (1989) is The Cure's masterpiece, the album where Robert Smith stopped fighting his reputation as rock's most miserable man and made a record of pure, magnificent gloom. Turning thirty and terrified of losing relevance, Smith wrote the album largely alone, emerging with songs that were slower, longer and more atmospheric than anything the band had done before. The record is built on a foundation of deep, churning bass lines, shimmering keyboards and washes of guitar, with Smith's baritone floating above it all, singing about endings: of relationships, of youth, of love itself. 'Lullaby' is a creepy nursery rhyme about a spider who comes to feed, 'Pictures of You' was written from photos of a lost relationship and has become one of the band's most beloved songs, and 'Plainsong' opens the record with eight minutes of building, glacial beauty. Released to huge success, it is the album that turned The Cure from an alternative cult into one of the biggest bands in the world, and its influence can be heard in everything from goth to shoegaze to modern indie.

name: Juju
teaser: Siouxsie and the Banshees 1981 — the album that perfected gothic post-punk. John McGeoch's guitar work is now taught in music schools; he used a flanger pedal so creatively that Johnny Marr called him the most inventive guitarist of his generation. Siouxsie Sioux wrote the lyrics in a single feverish week.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Spellbound' — the drum pattern is a 12/8 gallop that never stops. McGeoch's guitar harmonics at 2:15 sound like glass breaking in slow motion. Then 'Arabian Knights' — inspired by the Middle Eastern political turmoil of 1981, the song's tension never releases. McGeoch had a nervous breakdown shortly after the album.

synopsis: Juju (1981) is the album that perfected gothic rock, taking the darkness that had been lurking in post-punk and turning it into a full aesthetic. Siouxsie and the Banshees had been moving toward a darker, more theatrical sound, and on Juju they arrived: the record is full of tribal drumming, exotic and menacing guitar lines from the brilliant John McGeoch, and Siouxsie Sioux's commanding, sensual vocals singing about voodoo, werewolves, Halloween and the allure of the dark. 'Spellbound' is the band's signature single, a driving, hypnotic track built on a riff that still sounds like nothing else, while 'Arabian Knights' and 'Into the Light' show the band's command of atmosphere. The album was a commercial breakthrough and became a blueprint: the entire goth movement that followed, from the Cure to Sisters of Mercy to countless imitators, drew directly from this record. It is the sound of a band at the peak of its powers, confident enough to make darkness sound like fun.

name: Violator
teaser: Depeche Mode 1990 — the synth-pop band's pivot to stadium-sized dark electronic rock. Recorded across 8 studios in 4 countries. The album sold 7.5 million copies. The band's near-constant infighting during recording was captured on tape and later sampled into the album.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Enjoy the Silence' — Martin Gore wrote it as a ballad; Alan Wilder turned it into the disco-goth anthem by adding the beat without telling anyone. Then 'Personal Jesus' — the famous guitar riff was played by Gore on a Gretsch through a vintage amp, processed to sound like a synthesizer. The album made darkness danceable.

synopsis: Violator (1990) is the album where Depeche Mode stopped being a synth-pop band and became something bigger, darker and more human. Recorded across studios in several countries with Flood producing and Alan Wilder's meticulous arrangements, the album was built around the contrast between Martin Gore's brooding, sensual songs and Dave Gahan's increasingly powerful voice, which had grown from a boyish tenor into a full, commanding instrument. The singles were the biggest of their career: 'Personal Jesus', built on a bluesy guitar riff and lyrics inspired by the telephone confession lines of the American evangelist Oral Roberts, and 'Enjoy the Silence', a song about finding peace in a world of noise that became their biggest international hit. Around them, the album explored religion, obsession and submission in songs like 'Halo' and 'Waiting for the Night'. The record was released with striking Anton Corbijn imagery, and it turned Depeche Mode into stadium-filling stars in America. It is the sound of electronic music growing up, finding soul and menace in the machines.

name: Power, Corruption & Lies
teaser: New Order 1983 — the band's second album after Ian Curtis's suicide and their transition from Joy Division. Peter Saville designed the cover using a 19th-century French painting; the color-code wheel on the back became the band's visual signature. The album reconciled electronic music with post-punk.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Age of Consent' — the opening bassline is Peter Hook playing the melody high up on the neck, his signature technique. Then 'Blue Monday' — released as a standalone 12-inch single and not on the original UK album, it became the best-selling 12-inch single of all time and bankrupted Factory Records because the die-cut sleeve cost more to produce than the record sold for.

synopsis: Power, Corruption & Lies (1983) is the album where New Order emerged from the shadow of Joy Division and became the most important electronic band of their generation. After the suicide of singer Ian Curtis, the surviving members had kept playing under a new name, and on this, their second album, they completed the transformation: Bernard Sumner now sang in a plain, vulnerable voice, Peter Hook's bass played lead melodies high up the neck, and the band's love of dance music began to take over their sound. The album contains 'Blue Monday', which was released as a separate single, but the record itself is a seamless whole, its title taken from a painting of a bunch of flowers that Peter Saville used on the cover. Songs like 'Age of Consent', 'Your Silent Face' and 'The Village' mix melancholy and euphoria in a way nobody had done before, built on drum machines and sequencers that still sound futuristic. It is the album that bridged the gap between post-punk and dance music, and its influence on electronic pop is incalculable.

name: Ocean Rain
teaser: Echo and the Bunnymen 1984 — the album they declared would be 'the greatest album ever made' before a note was written. They recorded the strings with a 35-piece orchestra in a Paris studio built by Napoleon III. The confidence paid off: it's now considered their masterpiece.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Killing Moon' — Ian McCulloch wrote the lyric in a dream and woke up to scribble it down. The mandolin was played by a session musician who'd never heard the band before. Then 'Ocean Rain' — the strings were recorded in a single take because the orchestra had to catch a train. The album cover was shot in Carnglaze Caverns, an abandoned slate mine in Cornwall.

synopsis: Ocean Rain (1984) is the album where Echo and the Bunnymen made good on their grandest ambitions, recording with a full orchestra and declaring in the sleeve notes that it was 'the greatest album ever made'. The band had been building toward this sound for years, and the record opens with 'Silver', a shimmering, wintry song, before arriving at its centerpiece, 'The Killing Moon', a brooding epic built on a descending guitar line and Ian McCulloch's cavernous, romantic voice, which he has called his finest moment. The band recorded the album in Paris and Liverpool with an orchestra arranged by Adam Peters, and the strings and woodwinds give the record a cinematic grandeur that matched McCulloch's lyrical visions of dreams, drowning and destiny. Songs like 'Seven Seas' and 'The Yo Yo Man' add pop and mystery to the sweep. The band's prediction of greatness was not quite fulfilled, but the album became their best-selling record and a touchstone for everyone from U2 to Coldplay, proof that rock bands could dream as big as film scores.

name: Marquee Moon
teaser: Television 1977 — the CBGB scene's most musically ambitious band. Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd traded guitar solos like jazz musicians trading fours. The title track is 10 minutes of interlocking guitar lines that never repeat. The album was rejected by every major label before Elektra took a chance.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — Verlaine and Lloyd recorded their guitar solos facing each other in the studio, each one responding to the other's phrases in real time. Then 'Venus' — the riff sounds like it's walking upstairs, repeatedly trying and failing to resolve. Television made punk smart without making it less urgent.

synopsis: Marquee Moon (1977) is the album that proved punk could be as intricate and virtuosic as any music that came before it. Television were the most musically ambitious band of the New York CBGB scene, and their debut record, produced by Andy Johns, captured their live sound in all its glory: Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd's twin guitars interweaved in long, exploratory solos that owed more to jazz and free improvisation than to the three-chord rage of most punk bands. The ten-minute title track is the album's centerpiece, a song that builds through several movements, with the two guitarists trading phrases like a conversation in a language only they understood. 'See No Evil' and 'Friction' are tighter pop songs, but everything on the record shares the same searching, restless quality. Verlaine's lyrics were cryptic and poetic, full of urban imagery and existential dread. The album sold poorly at first, but it has grown in reputation ever since, and it is now regarded as one of the greatest guitar records ever made, an influence on everyone from R.E.M. to Wilco.

name: Lust for Life
teaser: Iggy Pop 1977 — recorded in Berlin with David Bowie producing. Iggy had just gotten clean from heroin; Bowie was about to record 'Heroes' in the same studio. The album was written and recorded in 8 days. The title track's famous drum beat was borrowed from the Motown standard 'You Can't Hurry Love' and later became the opening theme for Trainspotting.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Passenger' — Iggy wrote it riding the Berlin S-Bahn. The guitar riff was Bowie's idea, based on a Ricky Nelson song. Then 'Tonight' — Bowie later recorded his own version with Tina Turner, but Iggy's original, sung in a cracked baritone while barely holding a note, is the definitive take.

synopsis: Lust for Life (1977) is the album where Iggy Pop came back from the dead and made some of the most vital rock and roll of his career. After the collapse of the Stooges and years of heroin addiction, Iggy had been rescued by David Bowie, who brought him to Berlin, helped him get clean and produced this album, following up their collaboration on The Idiot the same year. The music is lean, tough and full of swagger, driven by the drumming of Hunt Sales and bass of Tony Sales, and Iggy's voice, a furious bark that could also turn tender, had never sounded more alive. The title track became one of rock's great anthems, later adopted by crowds at football games around the world, while 'Sixteen', 'Some Weird Sin' and 'Success' show the range of Iggy's new sound, mixing hard rock with the experimental edge of the Berlin scene. The album was a commercial failure at the time but has become a classic, and its influence on punk and alternative rock is enormous. It is the sound of a man choosing life.

name: Daydream Nation
teaser: Sonic Youth 1988 — a double album that made noise beautiful. The band used screwdrivers, drumsticks, and various objects wedged between guitar strings to create sounds no one had heard before. The album was picked as one of the first 50 recordings preserved in the Library of Congress's National Recording Registry.
